title: Walking God home
hookLine: the sky is dark with clouds, and Radha is told to take him home
carry: bhakti: the lord of all, close enough to love
tomorrow: Radha at the edge of the dance

cards: The sky is heavy with clouds. The forest is dark with tamala trees. Night is coming on, and the boy is nervous.
So Nanda, the cowherd chief, turns to Radha: take him home. That's how the Gita Govinda begins, with a walk home through the dark.
And the verse hails what follows on the bank of the river Yamuna: the secret love of Radha and Madhava, one of Krishna's names.
After our days on the Bhagavad Gita, the path turns from Krishna the teacher on a battlefield to Krishna the beloved in a forest.

teach.h: THE SONG OF GOVINDA, THE COWHERD.
teach.b: Gita Govinda means the song of Govinda, the cowherd, another name for Krishna. It's a love poem, and it says so up front. A few lines in, Jayadeva gives an invitation.
If your heart is moved by remembering Hari, and if you're curious about the arts of love, then listen to these sweet, soft, lovely words. Remembering God and the play of lovers, offered as one door.

teach.h: A HYMN TO THE LORD'S DESCENTS.
teach.b: Then, before the love story starts, Jayadeva sings a hymn through the Lord's descents into the world, the avatars: the fish, the tortoise, the boar, the man-lion, the dwarf, and on through Rama and the Buddha to Kalki, one stanza each.
Every stanza ends with the same refrain: jaya jagadisha hare, victory to you, Hari, Lord of the world.

teach.h: THE COSMIC LORD, THEN THE BOY.
teach.b: So the reader meets the cosmic Lord first, the one who saves worlds in many forms, and only then the nervous boy Radha is walking home under the clouds. Same Lord.

That's one of bhakti's boldest teachings, named plainly: the God of the whole universe comes close enough to be loved like a person, a child to be walked home, a beloved. You don't have to shrink God to love God up close.
For centuries the Gita Govinda has been sung in worship at the Jagannath temple in Puri, and Odissi dancers still perform its songs. Jayadeva doesn't explain the paradox. He just sings it.

how: The Gita Govinda has been sung in worship at the Jagannath temple in Puri for centuries; its songs are sung in Hindu devotional settings and performed in classical music and Odissi dance, and the hymn to the avatars with its refrain jaya jagadisha hare is sung on its own as well.

games.q: you're the poet. before the love story, you sing the Lord saving the world as a fish, a tortoise, a man-lion. why start there?
o: to show the boy in the forest is the same Lord of the whole world.
because the love story is too small to be about God.

games.why: Jayadeva praises the Lord in every descent, then shows him as the boy Radha walks home: in bhakti, the Lord of all comes close enough to love.

practice: Hear the opening again: clouds, dark trees, night coming, and Radha asked to walk the boy home. Now let two pictures sit side by side: the Lord of the whole world, fish, tortoise, man-lion, and the boy under the clouds.

If you pray, let the refrain move quietly with the breath, jaya jagadisha hare, the way it's still sung at home and in temples. If not, simply hold the two pictures together, something vast and someone near, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti. Devotion, loving attention. In the Gita Govinda, it's love for the Lord of the world, close enough to walk home.
